ostensible

/ah-STEN-suh-buhl/ - the stress falls on STEN · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Ostensible means stated as a reason, but not necessarily the real one.

Her ostensible reason for the 6 a.m. run was training; the bakery along the route told the fuller story.

Example

The dean announced that the new sign-in sheet outside the studio was about fire safety — an ostensible purpose nobody openly doubted. But the sheet appeared the same week the kilns began emptying overnight, and the only column anyone ever checked was who had been in the building after ten.

Ostensible neither accuses nor clears: it marks the gap between the reason shown and the reason held. Ostendere, 'to show,' does the work — the ostensible motive is the one held up for viewing. If you know the show is false, sham or pretended says so; ostensible keeps the question politely open.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

professed: Professed means declared aloud by the person concerned — a professed pacifist has said so herself, believe it or not. The word points at the act of announcing. Ostensible points at the gap between the reason shown and the reason held, and needs no announcement at all — only a surface.

purported: Purported passes along someone else's claim with a visible shrug — a purported Rembrandt is called that secondhand, by tellers who will not vouch for it. Ostensible is the observer's own cooler verdict on a stated reason: here is the version on display; the truth may sit elsewhere.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

genuine: the real thing

actual: what is truly so

Where it sits · how doubtful the stated reason is — declared → ostensible → sham

declared vs. ostensible: A declared purpose is simply the one on paper, no wink attached; ostensible raises the eyebrow.

sham vs. ostensible: A sham goes past ostensible: ostensible leaves room for the stated reason to be true, while a sham reason is false outright — a costume over the real one.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — ostens

Root — ostens: shown, displayed (Latin ostendere)

Suffix — -ible

Suffix — -ible: able to be

Put it together

Put it together: Ostens (shown, from Latin ostendere, 'to hold out for viewing') + -ible (able to be) = able to be shown — and, in practice, the version that is shown. The same root turned up the volume in ostentatious, where the showing becomes showing off. Ostensible stays quieter: it just reminds you that what is shown and what is true can be two different things.

Use the root in a new word: ostentatious

Use the root in a new word: ostentatious: You met ostentatious in Course 1: even the marina's oldest members found the new arrival's yacht ostentatious.

Word Choice

journalistic / knowing

Ostensible is the reporter's raised eyebrow: it marks the reason shown without ruling on the reason held. Softer than sham, which convicts, and cooler than supposed, which smirks, it suits filings, motives, and agendas — anywhere the show and the truth might differ.
